extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic/modern philosophy; philosophers and those studying semantics, ontology, and the theory of meaning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for classifying names and the kinds of things they denote (feelings, substances, attributes), and for distinguishing modes of predication (univocal, equivocal, analogical). Useful for doing careful philosophical or logical analysis of language and concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative name
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is relative when, over and above the object which it denotes, it implies in its signification the existence of another object deriving a denomination from the same fact which is the ground of the first name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent paraphrases on the page: a name is relative 'when, being the name of one thing, its signification can not be explained but by mentioning another' and 'when the name can not be employed in discourse so as to have a meaning, unless the name of some other thing ... be either expressed or understood.' Example: 'father' connotes the fact as an attribute of A and 'son' the same fact as an attribute of B. Note the analytic point that what matters is that the attribute grounded on a shared fact would disappear if only one individual existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal vs. Æquivocal (equivocal) use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is applied univocally with respect to all things of which it can be predicated in the same sense; it is equivocal when predicated in different senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity implies effectively two different names coinciding in sound. Examples: 'file' meaning a steel instrument vs. 'file' meaning a line of soldiers; 'grease' vs 'Greece' pronounced alike but different words. This criterion advises treating distinct senses as distinct names rather than confusing them as one ambiguous term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical or metaphorical use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name used analogically is predicated of two things not in exactly the same signification, but in somewhat similar, derivative senses — one primary, the other secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'brilliant' of a light and of an achievement. Anti-pattern: arguing from a metaphorical expression as if it were literal — i.e., treating a derivative signification as the original sense leads to fallacy. The text emphasizes that metaphorical uses are effectively different names in practice and warns about fallacious reasoning arising from ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition as joining of two names
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposition is discourse which affirms or denies something of some other thing; thus proof presupposes propositions, and propositions presuppose names (subjects and predicates) joined by a copula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basic logical criterion: to analyze what is provable one must know what names signify, because propositions operate by predicating one namable thing of another. Use this to justify enumerating kinds of Things that can be predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of 'Things' (Categories) capable of being predicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Before determining the import of predication, one should enumerate all kinds of Things which are capable of being made predicates or of having anything predicated of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical Aristotelian Categories are presented (substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, where, when, position, habitus) but criticized as redundant and defective. Guidance: prefer an analysis that penetrates to the 'rationale' of distinctions rather than a mere catalogue; beware omissions and repetitions in naive taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware ambiguity of general concrete terms (Thing, Being, Entity, Essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete names used to denote all that exists (Thing, Being, Entity, Essence) suffer from ambiguity, often drifting to connote substances and excluding attributes and feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for writers/analysts: understand the defects of the words you must employ; choose the term least likely to mislead in context; do not feel bound to one rigid sense when no single unambiguous term exists. The author defends occasional improper use of a term to call up helpful associations, but with explicit warning to avoid misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Feelings (states of consciousness) as a class of namable things
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings or states of consciousness are a primary class of namable things; in the broad sense they include Sensation, Emotion, Thought, and Volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'feeling' in enlarged sense to cover anything the mind is conscious of. Note that 'thought' is what passes in the mind itself (ideas, mental images), distinct from the external objects of thought. Sensations must be carefully distinguished from the objects that cause them and from attributes ascribed to objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sensation from object and attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation is not the object which causes it, nor the attribute ascribed to the object; language often conflates them but conceptually they are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sensation of white vs white object vs the attribute 'whiteness'. Note linguistic shortcoming: for many sensations we lack single-word names (except sound), so language often denotes both sensation and attribute with the same term (e.g., 'color'). Analysts should avoid conflation and be explicit when referring to sensation, attribute, or object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish bodily-organ states from sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the physical states of bodily organs (the physiological antecedents) from the sensation proper, which is a state of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophically there is no ground for a strict bodily/mental divide: sensations are states of mind though occasioned by bodily states. Confusing the bodily condition with the sensation leads to category errors. The division 'bodily vs mental feelings' often misconstrues that distinction: it's a distinction of causal agency, not of the nature of the feelings themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as an act of recognition (distinct from sensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is sometimes introduced as recognition of an external object as the cause of sensation — an act of the mind (intuitive belief) distinct from passive sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify perceptions among feelings/states of mind; treat perceptions as cases of belief that claim to be intuitive or independent of external evidence. The author notes that the lawfulness and legitimacy of intuitive belief belong to metaphysics or psychology, not to logic, but that perception should be considered among the varieties of feelings for logical classification purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volitions and action (action as volition + effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volitions (acts of the will) are active states of mind and form a principal part of many names' connotations; an action comprises a volition (intention) followed by an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: relational names (sovereign/subject, physician/patient) connote numerous actions; some names connote actions by persons other than those denoted (mortgagor/mortgagee connote judicial enforcement). Analysts should recognize that much of a name's connotation consists in actions under various contingencies, and that an action is logically analysable as intention + subsequent effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of body/substance as external cause of sensations (and its epistemic limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body (substance) may be defined as the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations; but there is philosophical controversy whether bodies are distinct from the sensations themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text sets out the idealist critique (objects as sets of sensations joined by laws) and the common reply: belief in matter is intuitive and practical. Guidance for analysis: recognize that 'all we know of objects is the sensations which they give us and the order of occurrence of those sensations' (Kantian/Berkeleyan point) and be explicit about which epistemic stance one adopts when invoking 'substance' in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of naive categorical lists (avoid mere catalogues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely listing high-level categories (as in traditional 'Categories' or 'Predicaments') without penetrating analysis yields redundancies, omissions, and verbal distinctions rather than principled ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends a more analytic approach to determine the true 'rationale' of distinctions; do not accept a catalogue (e.g., Aristotle's categories) uncritically—test whether items are genuinely distinct or repeated under different heads, and whether important kinds (e.g., feelings, states of mind) have been omitted.
